capturedContent.title: Starlight Festival on Nova Station
capturedContent.rawText: SUNNY SYNTHETIC LAB FIXTURE | LAB-MATH-C Festival Team Challenge Independent transfer across facts, arrays, and word problems Grade 3 mathematics Student: Synthetic Learner Date: 2026-08-08 Version: BLANK 1 A festival makes 7 teams with 6 children on each team. How many children? 2 Forty flags are placed in 5 equal rows. How many flags are in each row? 3 Fill in the missing factor: ___ x 8 = 48. 4 Write two multiplication equations represented by a 4-by-9 array. 5 Three booths each need 8 cups in the morning and 8 cups later. How many cups total? 6 Which story uses 6 x 7? A. 6 bags with 7 tokens each B. 6 tokens plus 7 tokens C. 7 tokens shared by 6 A B C 7 A child writes 5 x 9 = 40. Use a nearby fact to correct the answer. 8 A stage has 36 lights. Draw two different equal-row arrays that use all 36. Show your thinking. This document is synthetic and contains no real child data. LAB-MATH-C / original

nodes.targetLane: Given a contextual equal-groups situation with single-digit factors, state the factors, the product, and what each factor counts.
nodes.title: Arrival Dock: Lantern Parade Power-Up

rounds.prompt: Which equation matches this situation: 9 face-painting tables, each with 4 chairs?

nodes.mechanic: Each item is one parade scene: equal groups are drawn on screen as real festival objects (wagons of lanterns, packs of snacks, tables of chairs, trays of cups). The child answers by typing a number, tapping a matching equation, or speaking/typing a one-line explanation of what each factor counts. Every correct answer sends a visible amber pulse down a conduit and lights one dock district; the parade physically advances one wagon-length toward the festival gate.
nodes.engagementHypothesis: With no math evidence on record, the construct band can be probed to equal depth through either an array-first path (structure made visible as rows and columns before inverse work) or a story-first path (structure read out of contextual equal-groups language before inverse work). Both routes cover the same inverse/factor-pair demand at the same difficulty, so any performance difference isolates representational entry point rather than academic level.

nodes.targetLane: Given several stories using the same pair of numbers, select the one that matches a given multiplication expression and justify why the others are not equal-groups situations.
nodes.title: Arrival Dock: The Sorting Beacon

options.label: 8 baskets with 3 apples in each basket
9 rows of chairs with 5 chairs in each row
9 chairs plus 5 chairs brought from the truck

nodes.mechanic: For each item the beacon holds an expression card and three story-pods share the same number pair but different structures (equal groups, adding, sharing). The child taps a pod to feed it in. Matching pods lock in with a beam of amber light to a district; non-matching pods are gently rejected — the beacon holds them up and highlights the story words that broke the match. Two items ask for a short typed or spoken justification, entered on a simple two-tap sentence-builder plus free text.
nodes.engagementHypothesis: With no math evidence on record, the construct band can be probed to equal depth through either an array-first path (structure made visible as rows and columns before inverse work) or a story-first path (structure read out of contextual equal-groups language before inverse work). Both routes cover the same inverse/factor-pair demand at the same difficulty, so any performance difference isolates representational entry point rather than academic level.

nodes.targetLane: Retrieve or reliably derive multiplication facts with factors 2 through 9, with accuracy and hesitation recorded separately from structural performance.
nodes.title: Arrival Dock: Fuse Check
nodes.mechanic: Pure, calm fact entry: one fuse at a time, bare prompt, numeric answer, untimed. Each correct product snaps the fuse alight with a satisfying click and slides the next fuse into place. There is deliberately no narrative load here — the contrast with the story-rich nodes is itself the design, honoring the contract's separation of fact fluency from structure.
nodes.engagementHypothesis: With no math evidence on record, the construct band can be probed to equal depth through either an array-first path (structure made visible as rows and columns before inverse work) or a story-first path (structure read out of contextual equal-groups language before inverse work). Both routes cover the same inverse/factor-pair demand at the same difficulty, so any performance difference isolates representational entry point rather than academic level.

nodes.targetLane: Given a rectangular array, write both multiplication equations it represents and explain what the rows and columns each count.
nodes.title: Light Wall Wing: The Two-Way Lantern Rack

rounds.prompt: An array shows 4 rows of 9. Which equation does NOT describe this array?

nodes.mechanic: The child reads arrays as physical lantern grids and answers by building equations from drag tiles, typing totals, or explaining row/column roles. The signature move is the double-lighting: after the first equation lights the rack row-by-row (6 sweeps of 8), building the commuted equation re-lights the same rack column-by-column (8 sweeps of 6), proving on screen that both equations describe one object.
engagementDimensions: Whether a visual, build-a-grid entry (picture-first) holds this learner through the harder inverse and factor-pair items better than a narrative entry — testing the mixed-learning-style hypothesis with a concrete visual anchor.
nodes.engagementHypothesis: Because the chart records learningStyle=mixed with a visual component and no engagement history at all, a route that opens with a picture-like rectangular arrangement may give this learner a concrete anchor that keeps a moderate attention span on task through the harder inverse items.

nodes.targetLane: Given a total with several factor pairs within single-digit factors, produce two distinct equal-row arrangements that use the whole total and record the equation for each.
nodes.title: Light Wall Wing: Design the Launch Walls
nodes.mechanic: Freeform array construction with smart snapping: the child sets a row length by placing lanterns, then can duplicate rows with a stamp handle. A live counter shows lanterns used vs. budget (e.g., 21/24), and an equation strip auto-drafts beneath the build (e.g., '3 × 8 = ?') which the child must complete and sign. Uneven rows physically sag and spark, making 'equal rows using the whole total' a visible engineering constraint, not a rule to remember.
engagementDimensions: Whether a visual, build-a-grid entry (picture-first) holds this learner through the harder inverse and factor-pair items better than a narrative entry — testing the mixed-learning-style hypothesis with a concrete visual anchor.
nodes.engagementHypothesis: Because the chart records learningStyle=mixed with a visual component and no engagement history at all, a route that opens with a picture-like rectangular arrangement may give this learner a concrete anchor that keeps a moderate attention span on task through the harder inverse items.

nodes.targetLane: Given a total and one factor — presented either as an equation with an unknown or as an equal-rows sharing story within 48 — determine the missing factor and name the multiplication fact that verifies it.
nodes.title: Market Wing: The Stall-Keepers' Missing Numbers
nodes.mechanic: Each stall is one item: a keeper states a short problem aloud (text mirrored, tap-to-replay), and the child answers by dialing a number into an equation socket, typing a value, or — on the capstone — assembling the missing-factor equation themselves from socket parts before solving it and naming the verifying fact. Correct sockets close the stall's circuit: lights, music, and smell-wisps all switch on at once, and the keeper begins actually selling to the crowd.
engagementDimensions: Whether keeping every item inside one continuous market story (narrative-first) lowers switching cost and sustains attention across the inverse band better than the grid-building entry — testing whether text is a hook or a barrier for this learner.
nodes.engagementHypothesis: Because the source page is entirely festival-story framed and the chart shows no prior math engagement data, a route that keeps every item in a narrative situation may reduce the switching cost between reading the situation and doing the math, keeping a moderate-attention learner engaged across the inverse band.

nodes.targetLane: Given a story where equal groups each contribute a quantity on two occasions, compute the total and show the multiplicative structure used.
nodes.title: Market Wing: The Double-Shift Night
nodes.mechanic: Each item is a supply order for a two-occasion story. The child computes totals on the order-pad, and on structure items builds the delivery plan on a two-panel planning board — MORNING and AFTERNOON panels — by placing equation tiles (4 × 5 = 20 in each panel, then ×2 to the night total, or the combined 4 × 10 = 40 across both). Deliveries then physically run: hover-crates drop the ordered amount at each booth across both shifts, so an under-order is visible as afternoon booths left empty-handed.
engagementDimensions: Whether keeping every item inside one continuous market story (narrative-first) lowers switching cost and sustains attention across the inverse band better than the grid-building entry — testing whether text is a hook or a barrier for this learner.
nodes.engagementHypothesis: Because the source page is entirely festival-story framed and the chart shows no prior math engagement data, a route that keeps every item in a narrative situation may reduce the switching cost between reading the situation and doing the math, keeping a moderate-attention learner engaged across the inverse band.
